newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani love-match woman disappears - husband.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani love-match woman disappears - husband.

text.p: A 22-year-old Pakistani woman who won an 11-month court battle to uphold the validity of a love marriage opposed by her conservative Moslem father has disappeared, her husband said on Friday.
Arshad Ahmed and lawyers offered different versions of the latest twist in the saga of the tall, dark-haired student, Saima Waheed, whose whereabouts were unknown.
On Monday the Lahore High Court, in a split 2-1 verdict, said Saima was free to leave the women's shelter where she had stayed for 11 months under a court order and rejoin her husband.

The court ruled that their love marriage was valid in the eyes of Islam even though it occurred against the will of Saima's father, Abdul Waheed Ropri, a member of the militant Sunni Moslem Ahle Hadith organisation.
Several newspapers carried photographs of Saima and Ahmed's reunion the day after the court decision, showing the apparently overjoyed couple feeding each other pieces of cake.
Ahmed said he had gone to the office of Saima's lawyer Asma Jahangir on Thursday to collect his wife, but she had told him she was leaving with his own lawyer Abid Saqi instead.
"She said, 'Sorry Arshad, I am going with Abid'," Ahmed said, describing his wife as a "changed woman".
Saima then drove away in Saqi's car and went to the High Court, where she wrote an affidavit that she had left the shelter of her own free will, lawyers said.
Ahmed said he did not know where she had gone after that.
"Either my lawyer has handed over my wife to her parents after taking a bribe or they might have developed an understanding, but I have doubts about that," he said, without elaborating.
For his part, Saqi told Reuters he handed Saima over to her husband at his office in front of witnesses on Thursday. He denied newspaper reports that he had started a romantic liaison with her.
"I do not know where she is but I handed him Saima myself," he said. "Lawyers were there and so were four of his friends."
Jahangir could not explain the bizarre course of events.
"I don't know what is happening," said Jahangir, who is chairperson of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan.
"I think Saima might have returned (to her father)."
